subject: Climate & Environment
title: Mangrove Destruction
description: A quick win: understand Mangrove Destruction.

hook.text: Mangroves store four times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests. We've lost half of them.

buildup.text: These coastal trees thrive in saltwater, filtering pollution and sheltering fish nurseries.

discovery.text: Mangroves reduce wave energy by up to 66%, protecting coastal communities from storms and flooding.

twist.text: Shrimp farming has destroyed vast mangrove areas in Southeast Asia for cheap seafood exports.

climax.text: Restoring mangroves costs a fraction of building concrete sea walls — and works better.

punchline.text: The best coastal defense is a tree that grows in the sea.

quiz.question: How much carbon do mangroves store compared to rainforests?

details.summary: Mangroves are coastal trees that protect shorelines from storms, nurture fish nurseries, and store up to four times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests. Despite their value, mangrove forests have shrunk by over a third since the 1980s, cleared mainly for shrimp farms and development.
details.whyItMatters: Mangrove loss removes a natural coastal defense and releases stored carbon. Protecting and restoring mangroves is one of the most cost-effective climate and disaster-resilience strategies available.
takeaways: Mangroves store up to four times more carbon than rainforests
Over a third of mangrove forests have been lost since the 1980s
They protect coastlines and serve as fish nurseries

faq.question: Why are mangroves so effective at storing carbon?
faq.answer: Mangrove soils are waterlogged and low in oxygen, which slows decomposition. Carbon from fallen leaves and roots accumulates in thick layers of peat that can lock away carbon for thousands of years, far longer than typical forest soils.

faq.question: What is driving mangrove destruction?
faq.answer: Aquaculture, especially shrimp farming, is the leading cause, followed by coastal development, agriculture, and pollution. Southeast Asia has suffered the greatest losses. Some countries have enacted protections, but enforcement remains weak.
